William Bridge
WIL-yum BRIJ
proper noun
English given name William, from the Germanic Wilhelm, “resolute protector”; the surname Bridge from the Old English brycg, a crossing over water.

📖 Biblical Definition

William Bridge (c.1600–1671) was a Puritan minister and one of the divines summoned to the Westminster Assembly, where he stood among the “dissenting brethren” who pressed the Congregational way of church order against the Presbyterian majority. Educated at Cambridge, he fled to Holland under Laudian persecution and pastored an English congregation at Rotterdam before returning to labor at Yarmouth. Though he differed with his brethren on polity, he was one with them in the doctrines of grace and in warm experimental godliness. His most enduring work, A Lifting Up for the Downcast, is a treasury of comfort for the cast-down believer, addressing the soul discouraged by sin, by affliction, by desertion, by want of assurance, and by the wickedness of the heart. Bridge brings the promises of God to bear upon each particular grief, insisting that no condition of the saint lies beyond the reach of Christ’s sufficiency. He held that discouragement dishonors God by doubting His faithfulness, and so he labored to lift the eyes of the weary from their wounds to their Physician. A faithful preacher and a tender pastor, Bridge embodies the Puritan gift of joining doctrinal precision to the cure of troubled consciences, pointing fainting pilgrims to the unfailing grace that sustains them to the end.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Puritan minister and Westminster divine of the Congregational party, author of A Lifting Up for the Downcast.

expand to see more

WILLIAM BRIDGE, English Puritan minister (c.1600–1671), educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.

Fled to Rotterdam under Laudian persecution, returning to pastor at Great Yarmouth.

One of the divines of the Westminster Assembly and a leader of the Congregational “dissenting brethren.”

Author of A Lifting Up for the Downcast, a classic of pastoral comfort for the discouraged soul.

He taught that no affliction of the saint lies beyond the sufficiency of Christ (2Co 4:8).

📖 Key Scripture

Psa 42:11 — "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God."

2Co 4:8 — "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;"

Isa 40:31 — "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Mat 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Bridge’s ministry of comfort is recovered against a therapeutic age that treats discouragement as a chemical problem rather than a matter for the promises of God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Bridge’s pastoral work confronts the modern habit of reducing every cast-down soul to a mere imbalance to be medicated, severed from God, conscience, and the promises of Scripture. Bridge did not deny real affliction; he addressed it with the whole counsel of God, naming the soul’s discouragements one by one and answering each with the sufficiency of Christ. To lift the downcast by the gospel is a richer cure than the world’s, for it touches the spirit and not merely the frame.

The lesson to recover is that discouragement, however heavy, is no place beyond the reach of grace, and that to doubt God’s faithfulness dishonors Him. Bridge teaches the weary believer to argue with his own soul as the psalmist did, to hope in God, and to wait upon the LORD who renews the strength of the faint. The remedy for the downcast is not within the self but above it, in the unfailing mercy of Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

William means “resolute protector”; Bridge denotes a crossing, a fitting name for one who pointed souls over from despair to hope.

expand to see more

William — from Germanic Wilhelm, “will” joined to “helmet,” hence “resolute protector.”

Bridge, from Old English brycg, a structure spanning water.

Downcast, from down and cast, the soul thrown low, as in “cast down” (Psa 42:11).

Comfort, from the Latin confortare, “to strengthen greatly,” not merely to soothe.

Dissenting, from the Latin dissentire, “to differ in judgment,” as Bridge dissented on church order.

Usage

"William Bridge wrote to lift up the souls that affliction had cast down."

"Among the Westminster divines, William Bridge contended for the Congregational way."

"When despair pressed hard, the saints found in William Bridge a faithful physician of the soul."
